episode.throughLine: A short documentary vignette of an urgent patent deadline, completed paperwork that needed correction, and eventual grant. No reconstruction of private fear, rejection for beauty or a personal awakening.

facts.statement: Lamarr was twenty-seven on 13 April 1942, based on her birth on 9 November 1914.
Her lawyers' 13 April 1942 letter requested immediate attention, warned that delaying the affidavit and payment could mean loss of the patent, and offered execution before their office notary.

sourceRefs.locator: Page 2, paragraph beginning We cannot urge you too strongly.

facts.statement: The 13 April letter stated that the final government fee must be paid before 13 May, and the affidavit must precede payment by twenty days.
By 16 April 1942 Lamarr had signed the required affidavit, which her lawyers sent to their Washington associates with a request to obtain the necessary certified copy quickly.

sourceRefs.locator: Paragraph beginning We enclose TFR Form 172.

facts.statement: On 16 April the lawyers acknowledged her thirty-dollar check for the government's final fee.
An 18 April telegram reported that the signature's name did not match the name in the application and requested another correctly signed form.

sourceRefs.locator: Telegram body, beginning Certified copy ordered.

facts.statement: On 18 April the lawyers sent Walton another affidavit to have signed with the name matching the application.
On 18 April the lawyers told their associates they enclosed a new affidavit properly executed by Hedy Kiesler Markey.
Patent 2,292,387 was issued to Hedy Kiesler Markey and George Antheil on 11 August 1942 with six claims.
The patent describes changing radio frequencies together at transmitter and receiver to make interference harder.
Hedy Lamarr was an actor and co-inventor of the patented radio communication system.

sourceRefs.locator: Career and patent sections; name cross-check in original patent.

arc.canonicalText: A letter addressed to her warned that delay could cost her the patent. She was twenty-seven.
arc.sourceNote: Document itself is the opening; no asserted reading moment. User-authorized short source-led format; FOR OWNER READING, not approved.

arc.canonicalText: Her lawyers needed a signed affidavit before they could arrange the final government payment. The deadline was approaching.
arc.sourceNote: Documented practical threat, not an invented emotion. User-authorized short source-led format; FOR OWNER READING, not approved.

arc.canonicalText: She signed the form and supplied a check for the final fee. Her lawyers sent the paperwork onward.
arc.sourceNote: Attested acts summarized, without a signing scene. User-authorized short source-led format; FOR OWNER READING, not approved.

arc.canonicalText: A telegram then reported that her signature did not match the name on the application. Her lawyers requested another signed form. The first one needed correcting.
arc.sourceNote: Specific unsuccessful paperwork step; no personal shame inferred. User-authorized short source-led format; FOR OWNER READING, not approved.

arc.canonicalText: Her lawyers reported that a replacement form had been correctly signed and was being sent onward. They had addressed the mismatch.
arc.sourceNote: Attributed contemporaneous report, not independent inspection of a replacement affidavit. User-authorized short source-led format; FOR OWNER READING, not approved.

arc.canonicalText: The patent was granted later that summer, naming her and her collaborator as the inventors. Their proposed system aimed to make radio communication harder to interfere with. Both inventors were credited.
arc.sourceNote: Grant, not proof of adoption or successful deployment. User-authorized short source-led format; FOR OWNER READING, not approved.

arc.canonicalText:
Her name was Hedy Lamarr.

She was an actor who also helped invent a radio communication system.

Your life is not theirs.

But a piece of this story may still sit beside you.

You do not have to explain every part of yourself.

You are allowed to want your work taken seriously.
